title: Relationships · Episode 1
chapters: Siblings: the longest relationship of your life

units.t: Relationships. Episode one.
In this episode: Attachment styles, The power of touch, Siblings: the longest relationship of your life and The science of love.
Part one. Attachment styles.
The bonds you formed as a baby may echo in how you love as an adult, though less rigidly than the internet suggests.
Bowlby's big idea.
In the 1950s, British psychiatrist John Bowlby challenged the popular idea that babies attach to their mothers mainly because they provide food.
Drawing on work with children separated from their families, including children in hospitals and institutions, he argued that humans have an evolved attachment system.
Infants seek closeness to caregivers, especially when frightened, tired or sick, because staying near protectors helped survival.
A caregiver who responds reliably becomes a 'secure base' from which the child can explore the world.
Harry Harlow's ethically troubling experiments, in which infant monkeys clung to soft cloth 'mothers' rather than wire ones holding milk, supported similar ideas.
The Strange Situation.
Mary Ainsworth, who worked with Bowlby, designed the Strange Situation in the 1970s.
A toddler of about one plays in an unfamiliar room, the parent leaves briefly, a stranger enters, and the parent returns.
Most children were upset but quickly comforted on reunion, then went back to play: securely attached.
Others were very distressed and hard to soothe, sometimes angry, anxious or ambivalent, or seemed indifferent and avoided the parent, avoidant.
Mary Main and Judith Solomon later identified a disorganised pattern, with children confused or frightened.
Sensitive, responsive caregiving makes secure attachment more likely, but the link is moderate: temperament, stress, poverty and health matter too.
Secure attachment is the most common pattern across countries, about 60 per cent in many samples, and babies also bond with fathers, grandparents and other carers.
Attachment in adult love.
In 1987, Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver applied attachment ideas to adult love, using a 'love quiz' printed in a newspaper.
Secure adults find it fairly easy to get close, depend on partners and be depended on.
Anxious adults crave closeness but fear abandonment, seek reassurance and may read a slow reply as a bad sign.
Avoidant adults feel uncomfortable with closeness, value independence and may shut down in emotional conversations.
Researchers now measure two scales, anxiety and avoidance, so most people are a mix.
The two can lock into a pursue-withdraw cycle: the anxious partner chases closeness, the avoidant partner feels crowded and pulls away, and the chasing intensifies.
Seeing it as a pattern you create together, and stating needs clearly, 'I feel reassured when you text if you're running late', helps break it.
Repair and change.
Secure attachment doesn't require perfect parents.
Donald Winnicott coined the phrase 'good enough mother' in the 1950s for care that meets a child's needs reasonably well.
Edward Tronick found that even healthy parent-baby pairs are often out of sync; what matters is how reliably mismatches get repaired.
In his 'still face' experiment, babies grew distressed when a parent's face went blank, then recovered when warm contact returned.
Adult relationships work the same way: ruptures are normal, and repair builds trust.
Attachment is moderately stable but not destiny.
Many people develop 'earned security' through a supportive relationship, good therapy or reflecting on early experiences.
Research with the Adult Attachment Interview suggests how coherently people tell their childhood story matters more than whether it was easy.
Using it wisely.
Attachment theory is well supported by decades of research, but online it's often oversimplified into rigid types used to label exes or diagnose dates after a few messages.
It isn't a clinical diagnosis, and a single quiz can't capture something that varies across relationships and over time.
It's most useful as a mirror: noticing your own patterns, like reassurance-seeking or pulling away when things get close, and choosing how to respond.
The qualities linked to secure relationships can be practised by anyone: responsiveness, reliability, honesty about needs, and repair after conflict.
If old patterns feel stuck, a psychologist or couples counsellor can help.
The key idea: Infants have an evolved need to stay close to caregivers for safety, and a responsive caregiver becomes a secure base.
Part two. The power of touch.
Your skin has nerve fibres that seem to exist mainly to register a caring stroke.
Touch is one of the first languages we learn, and one we never stop needing.
The first sense.
Touch is the first sense to develop in the womb, and for a newborn it is a primary way of experiencing the world.
Being held, rocked and stroked helps regulate a baby's temperature, breathing and heart rate, and calms distress.
In the 1950s Harry Harlow's infant rhesus monkeys clung to a soft cloth mother rather than a wire one that provided milk.
The experiments are now considered cruel, but they helped overturn the idea that babies attach to carers simply because carers feed them.
In 1978 in Bogotá, Colombia, paediatrician Edgar Rey Sanabria faced an incubator shortage and began having mothers hold premature babies skin-to-skin on their chests.
Called kangaroo mother care, it can improve survival, warmth, breathing, feeding and weight gain.
The World Health Organization recommends it, and skin-to-skin contact is common in Australian hospitals.
Nerves made for caress.
Skin is packed with sensors for pressure, vibration, temperature and pain.

In the late twentieth century, Scandinavian researchers including Åke Vallbo and Håkan Olausson studied a slow-conducting nerve fibre in human hairy skin, such as the arm and back, called C-tactile afferents.
These respond most strongly to gentle stroking at roughly the speed of a caress, a few centimetres per second, and at about skin temperature.
They seem linked to the pleasant, emotional feeling of touch rather than to identifying textures or shapes.
In one striking case, a patient who had lost the large nerve fibres that carry ordinary touch information could still faintly detect gentle stroking and report it as pleasant.
Our bodies appear to have a dedicated channel for affectionate touch.
Touch speaks.
In a 2006 study led by psychologist Matthew Hertenstein, pairs of strangers sat either side of a barrier, unable to see each other.
One put an arm through, and the other tried to communicate specific emotions only by touching the forearm.
Receivers identified anger, fear, disgust, love, gratitude and sympathy well above chance.
Each had a typical touch: love was often stroking, sympathy patting, gratitude shaking hands, and anger hitting or squeezing.
Brief touches can also shift behaviour.
In a 1984 restaurant experiment by April Crusco and Christopher Wetzel, diners lightly touched on the hand or shoulder by a waitress tended to leave larger tips than those not touched.
Hugs and health.
Touch from a trusted person can damp the body's stress response.

In experiments where women faced the threat of a mild electric shock in a brain scanner, holding their husband's hand reduced activity in threat-related brain regions, and the effect was stronger in happier marriages.
In a 2015 study led by psychologist Sheldon Cohen, around 400 healthy adults reported how often they were hugged, then were deliberately exposed to a common cold virus and monitored in quarantine.
Those who received more frequent hugs and had more social support tended to have less severe symptoms if they got sick.
The study cannot prove hugs caused this, since huggers may differ in other ways, but it fits a wider pattern linking warm contact with health.
Culture, consent and need.
Norms around touch differ widely.
In an often-quoted informal 1960s study, psychologist Sidney Jourard counted café couples touching in an hour: very high in San Juan and Paris, very low in Florida and none in London.
It was small, but later research also finds big differences between countries and relationships.
Whatever the culture, touch helps only when wanted.
Unwanted touch triggers stress, and people, including children, may decline a hug.
Asking 'Do you want a hug?'
costs nothing.
Some people, especially those who live alone, older people and the isolated, go weeks without kind touch.
'Touch starvation' is an everyday phrase, not a diagnosis, but surveys link lack of touch with loneliness.
Welcome hugs, holding hands, massage, sport, dancing, patting a pet or a hand on the chest can all help.
The key idea: Touch develops first and is central to how babies bond, grow and survive, as kangaroo care shows.
Part three. Siblings: the longest relationship of your life.
Your brothers and sisters often share more years of your life than your parents, partner or children do.
Here is what research says about rivalry, birth order myths, only children and why sibling bonds matter so much.
The longest relationship.
Who will be around for your whole life?
Parents usually die before us, and partners and friends tend to arrive later.
Siblings can share almost every chapter, from childhood bath times to retirement, often across seven or eight decades.
Siblings share parents, homes, family jokes and memories nobody else holds.
They can be best friends, fierce rivals, or both on the same day.
Researchers have long focused on parents and partners, but interest in siblings is growing.
These relationships shape how we learn to share, fight, negotiate and love, and they often matter more in old age than people expect.
Rivalry and training.
Sibling conflict is extremely common in childhood; studies of young siblings at home have recorded squabbles many times a day, often over parents' time and approval.
Lasting resentment seems to come less from conflict itself than from differential treatment: children believing a parent favours one of them.
What matters most is often whether the difference seems fair.
Extra homework help for a younger child may be accepted, while unexplained favouritism lingers.
Parents who explain their reasons and avoid comparisons can ease rivalry.
For all the fighting, siblings give daily practice at sharing, standing up for yourself and making up.
Warm sibling bonds are linked with better emotional understanding, and a supportive sibling can buffer family stress.
Ongoing bullying by a sibling is harmful, though, and shouldn't be dismissed as normal rivalry.
The birth order myth.
Popular wisdom says firstborns are bossy achievers, middle children are overlooked peacemakers, and youngest children are charming, rebellious and spoiled.
It is a satisfying story, and most of us can think of examples.
But in large samples the effects mostly vanish.
A 2015 study by German psychologists Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff and Stefan Schmukle used data from over twenty thousand people in Germany, the United States and the United Kingdom.
It found no meaningful birth order effects on traits such as extraversion, agreeableness or conscientiousness.
It did find a very small average advantage for firstborns on intelligence measures, far too small to matter for any individual.
The stereotypes persist because they make tidy stories, and we remember the examples that fit.
Why siblings differ.
Many parents marvel at how different their children are, despite the same home and the same parents.
Siblings share, on average, about half of their genetic variation, so there is plenty of room for difference.
Research also points to the non-shared environment: experiences that differ between siblings, such as different friends, teachers, hobbies, illnesses or even different treatment by parents.
Scientists find that much of the environmental influence on personality comes from these, not from the family home as a whole.
A family is not one environment but several.
Each child arrives at a different time with a different temperament, and parents change over the years.
Siblings may also carve out different niches, one the sporty one and another the bookish one, to stand out.
Only children and adult siblings.
Only children have long had a bad reputation.
In the late nineteenth century the American psychologist G. Stanley Hall reportedly called being an only child a disease in itself.
Later research, including reviews by Toni Falbo, has generally found only children are much like others on personality, sociability and adjustment.
Differences are small, and some favour only children, such as slightly higher achievement.
They gain social skills through cousins, friends and school.
In adulthood, sibling contact often drops as careers and families take over, yet many bonds warm again in midlife and old age.
Caring for ageing parents can bring siblings together, or reignite tensions over fairness and money.
Some relationships do break down.
If you have drifted from a sibling, a small step, like sharing an old photo, can reopen the door.
The key idea: Siblings can share more of your life than parents, partners or friends, so the bond matters.
Part four. The science of love.
Chemistry, psychology and a famous 36 questions.
What researchers have learned about falling, and staying, in love.
Love on the brain.
In a 2005 study, Helen Fisher, Arthur Aron and colleagues scanned people newly and intensely in love as they viewed photos of their beloved.
Dopamine-rich regions, including the ventral tegmental area and parts of the caudate nucleus, became more active: the same reward circuitry that responds to food, winning money and some drugs.
That helps explain the obsessive thinking, energy and craving of early love, and why rejection can feel like withdrawal.
Scans of recently rejected lovers also showed activity in reward and craving regions.

Fisher proposed three systems: lust, driven by hormones like testosterone and oestrogen; attraction, linked to dopamine and focused on one person; and attachment, linked to oxytocin and vasopressin, which creates the calm bond that helps partners stay together.
They can occur separately.
It's a useful model, not settled fact.
Who we fall for.
We tend to fall for people we see often: classmates, coworkers, neighbours, teammates.
A 1950 study of MIT student housing by Leon Festinger and colleagues found friendships formed most often between people living closest together.
Repeated exposure increases liking, the mere-exposure effect.
We favour people similar in values, background and interests; 'opposites attract' gets little research support.
We also like people who like us back.
Looks matter most at first meetings and less as people get to know each other.
Closeness can be built, too.
In 1997, Arthur Aron's team had pairs of strangers spend 45 minutes taking turns through 36 increasingly personal questions, from light ones to memories, regrets and problems.
Pairs felt much closer than those making small talk.
The aim was closeness, not romance, and it works for friendships too.
Culture, passion and time.
Some claim romantic love was invented by medieval European poets.
The evidence disagrees.

In 1992, William Jankowiak and Edward Fischer searched ethnographic records from 166 cultures and found clear evidence of romantic love in about 89 per cent, with most of the rest lacking enough information.
Love poems survive from ancient Egypt.
What differs is how much weight love gets when choosing a partner: in some societies families lead matchmaking and love is expected to grow after marriage.
Passionate love, the intense early longing, usually declines over the first few years.
Companionate love, a deep friendship of trust, affection and shared life, can keep growing, and many long-married couples report high satisfaction.
Robert Sternberg's 1986 triangular theory mixes intimacy, passion and commitment; consummate love combines all three.
Novelty and excitement.
Arthur Aron's self-expansion theory proposes that we're drawn to partners who broaden our lives, and that relationships feel most alive when they keep adding new experiences.
In a 2000 study, couples who crossed a gym-mat obstacle course while strapped together at the wrist and ankle reported greater relationship satisfaction afterwards than couples given a mundane task.
A famous 1974 experiment by Donald Dutton and Aron, on a swaying suspension bridge in Canada, suggested people can partly mistake the arousal of fear or excitement for attraction.
The practical lesson: keep trying new things together, from a hike to a cooking class.
What keeps couples together.
Psychologist John Gottman observed thousands of couples in his University of Washington 'love lab'.
Stable couples responded to each other's 'bids' for attention, like a comment about a bird outside or a hand on the shoulder, far more often than couples who later split.
In one study of newlyweds, those still together six years later had turned towards bids about 86 per cent of the time, versus about 33 per cent for those who divorced.
Stable couples also kept around five positive interactions for every negative one during conflict.
Gottman identified contempt, such as eye-rolling and mockery, as the strongest predictor of breakups.
Everyday kindness matters more than grand gestures.
The key idea: Early romantic love activates the brain's dopamine reward system, and Fisher proposed three overlapping systems: lust, attraction and attachment.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do infants seek closeness to caregivers, according to Bowlby?
Answer. Because staying near protectors helped survival.
Question two. What did Harlow's monkey experiments help overturn?
Answer. The idea that babies bond with carers only for food.
Question three. Why are siblings often described as the longest relationship of a person's life?
Answer. They can share most of life, from childhood to old age.
Question four. What does early romantic love activate in the brain?
Answer. The dopamine reward system, as with food or money.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
